author: Mya Clark
title: Food insecurity across High Plains remains prevalent according to study - NewsBreak
text:
By Mya Clark ,
3 hours ago
AMARILLO, Texas (KAMR/KCIT) — Feeding America released the 2026 Map the Meal Gap study, giving insight to food insecurity across the country and region.
According to the study:
1 in 5 people in the Texas Panhandle experienced food insecurity in 2024 1 in 4 children experienced food insecurity Swisher County has the regions highest estimated food insecurity at 25.4% 22.4% of Potter County residents and 30.7% of children experienced food insecurity More than 55% of people facing hunger in the Texas Panhandle have incomes too high to qualify for federal nutrition assistance High Plains Food Bank Executive Director Zack Wilson shared out of the 29 counties they serve, 11have food insecurity rates over 20%. Wilson attributed some of the data from 2024 to natural disasters that impacted the High Plains.
Texas lawmakers debate whether grid needs more gas generation as demand surges “The rising costs of everything these days have forced a lot of families, working families into making decisions that they’ve never made before,” explained Wilson. “And those that have been in that scenario before are now continuing to make those choices and even harder choices.”
According to Wilson although the availability of work and wages may have gone up over the past six years, it’s not to the extent that expenses have surpassed them.
“As we know now, fuel costs have gone up, but we have insurance, food costs, utilities, everything just has skyrocketed,” said Wilson. “And so you couple that with the ongoing problem that we have in our area and in a lot of places is food deserts, access to food, and healthy nutritious food on top of that and you really get what we’re going up against.”
Amarillo College says data center growth creating new opportunities for students Founder and Executive Director for Snack Pak 4 Kids Dyron Howell shared when surveying kids they serve a common issue is the reoccurring cause for food insecurity.
“When we survey our kids every year, you know what they tell us? Economics is the challenge that they see at home as to why they’re food insecure,” explained Dowell. “So, I think you can take that and be distracted, or you can lean into that and do what we’ve been doing for 16 years, which is serving thousands of kids in our area over the weekend.”
In the annual AISD K-8 teacher survey conducted by Snack Pak 4 Kids, 65% of educators reported seeing improvement in academic performance when kids were fed and ready for school. Additionally, 68% of educators reported seeing improved confidence in students when their basic needs are met.
“So, it’s one thing to say it,” said Howell. “It’s another thing for our teachers to say. This is what we see. And then I think there’s also this sense of belonging. I’m seen. I’m not invisible. I’m not a number. I think sometimes we throw out numbers like one and four, yet we forget about stories.”
West Texas A&M University receives $400,000 for nursing program from state Howell shared that he recently encountered a young man who helped him fix his taillight, and when the young man recognized the Snack Pak 4 Kids logo.
Howell continued, “he said that you fed me when I was a kid. In fact, you continue to feed me. He was a senior this past year at Amarillo High School. So, I think a lot of times we say one in four, and we forget that if we will invest, you know what the young man did? Hand me a business card. Has his own business. What he was trying to tell, and what I think a lot of our kids are trying to tell us is, if you’ll give us the tools we need, if you’ll recognize there’s something missing, we can make a difference in this world.”
While food insecurity continues to be a concern across the country and region, Wilson shared there is a solution.
“It’s a combination of food distribution, emergency food distribution, meeting needs where folks currently are, but also sustainability on an ongoing basis,” said Wilson. “And that’s where benefit assistance programs come into play. If we were to completely try to help meet those needs in the panhandle just by food distribution alone, it just couldn’t be done.”
Regardless of what led to an individual or family becoming food insecure for HPFB and Snack Pak 4 Kids shared they are ready to continue providing assistance and doing so with dignity.
“I’ve had business leaders walk in my door that were these kids that were judged, evaluated, questioned, made to feel less than,” explained Howell. So, they didn’t have dignity. They got served, but everything else was robbed from them. And so, what we found is when we invest in dignity and respect, it’s truly a priceless gift we give our kids for the rest of their life
